A couple of comments on the column:

First of all, as one with plenty of glassware, I'd still never think of them for the clue [Alternatives to coupes].  SEDANS, yes; even hatchbacks, SUVs, minivans or station wagons.  Coupes as glassware would never cross my mind in a million years.  Would have only been a tricky clue for me if it HAD been about glassware.

Secondly, I'd bet most baseball fans and even most Ohioans not near Toledo would recognize the MUD HENs.  This team is best known because Corporal Klinger on MASH, who was from Toledo, mentioned them frequently.  And the MASH finale, with 106 million viewers, was the most-watched scripted TV show ever in American history.  

Younger people now accustomed to so many more options may not be able to conceive of how popular certain TV shows were at some time.  But back in the day, everyone knew MASH.

As a retired otolaryngologist I always feel it is useful to respond to clues (22A) that touch upon my admittedly small field. People my be interested to know that the actual name of the “hammer” bone is the malleus. The ear drum (tympanic membrane) rests upon the portion of the malleus called the manubrium, and vibrations of that membrane are transmitted from the malleus through the incus and stapes into the inner ear. Part of that inner ear has tiny hair cells that respond to those vibrations and send signals to the brain that we process as sound.
And those bones are really really tiny.

But the two highlights today for me were:

•	The theme. Peter Gordon is an endless fount of colorful/original themes.  I could just see his brain ticking away after seeing “non-sporting group”.  This theme has never been done before, and is so clever.
•	A post solve marvelous TIL, when I went down a “non-sporting group” rabbit hole and learned that there are 20 AKC non-sporting breeds.  When I looked them over, I found one I’ve never heard of, and what a striking name – Xoloitzcuintli!  Some are hairless, some are not, and both can be in the same litter.  The shortened name is Xolo (pronounced show-low), and the full name comes from Nahuatl, an Aztec language.  Mwah to this TIL!

Nice to see AKRON so close to ACME, as the name "Akron," in Summit County, derives from the Greek adjective for "high" (Think "Acropolis."). It was the highest point, in elevation, along the Ohio-Erie Canal, at the divide between the Tuscaroras/Allegheny/Mississippi and Cuyahoga/St. Lawrence watersheds. (Although the actual First Nations portage was nearer to Canton, OH, in, um, Portage County.) And SMYRNA! I've been to the latter, but not the former. Later in his life, Tom turned to painting, initially as a form of art therapy, but then kept at it. Here's one of his canvases, which celebrates his home town: https://thomasbrodhead.com/theme/all-works/smyrnica While you're on his website, check out "Numbers Up," the game he designed. Warning--there will be math! His website is still up and running, but sadly Tom has been gone several years; His "Chromapotheosis" hangs proudly on my living room wall. I miss him, daily.

If you’d allow me to nerd out briefly, EDU is decidedly _not_ a common ending for URLs.

A quick (Gemini-assisted) google reveals that of the ~400 *million* domains registered, about ~20 *thousand* of them are under .edu (serendipitously, that also comes out to 1 in every 20 thousand domains).

One of the reasons it is so uncommon is because that top-level domain is restricted to accredited institutions (like colleges and universities).

Signed, your friendly neighborhood engineer / tech guy.

About "girl math", I have opinions! Your link starts with "Is this viral TikTok trend lightheartedly silly, or is girl math furthering stereotypes?" Um, furthering stereotypes, and why is that something women love to do? How could it be lighthearted when it's saying girls can't handle money?

1. Basic math is not a difficult skill to master, and like anything, you need to repeat it so you don't forget how. Ignorance of math has become something people think is cool. I've been pleasantly surprised to see French wait staff quickly divide up a bill in their heads. Granted, tax isn't a separate line item, but it's impressive, and almost all of them are good at it. Trust me, few people in the US can do that now. I owned a retail shop with (over 15 years), several hundred employees. Even simple addition paralyzed the vast majority. That sort of fear is taught.

2. Women are not bad at handling money. Studies show that women, on average, outperform men in investment returns. Back to the retail shop, which sold ice cream and chocolates: my experience is that women are much more price-sensitive than men. Women were our core customers with a few notable exceptions. Men shopped by themselves when they took the kids out for ice cream and on Valentine's Day. Typically they paid no attention to how much something cost. It was very easy to see as the seller.

3. "Girls" do not budget, they get allowances. Grown-@$$ women deal with finances. Calling an adult a girl is trivializing.

And one more thing—commercials. We didn’t mind them so much, they would come 3-4 breaks an hour, gave us time to get up for a snack and the restroom, usually weren’t repetitive, and at least came during predictable breaks in the action. Then we could fast forward them on VHS or TIVO and were rid of them for a while on cable or streaming. But of course now they’re back on most services unless you pay more. Which I wouldn’t mind but they pop up randomly with movies often at the most awkward dramatic moments, and usually the same commercials every break. And don’t get me started as a physician about the rise of pharmaceutical commercials for every disease no matter how rare or inappropriate. Sigh.

Yes I have noticed that we have come almost full circle. We went from low resolution pictures with lots of commercials through VHS and DVR and at the apex ad-free shows in glorious definition when the streamers were in their burning cash phase. Now we have settled back to lower quality with plenty of ads for most users. 

I too am amazed by the pharma ads when I visit the US. It's a completely alien concept to me that I would "ask my doctor" about a given brand of treatment when they have trained as an expert in the field for decades.

Part of the charm was because of the schedule, so many people were watching the same thing and could chat about it the next morning at work/school.

Similarly, life was better when everyone was tuned in to CBS, NBC or ABC news...shared reality had a lot going for it!
